The cell reaction uses the \(Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}\) couple, which is not given directly and must be built from the two iron half-reactions through free energies (potentials are not additive, \(\Delta G\) is).

For \(Fe^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow Fe\), \(\Delta G_{1} = -3Fz\).
For \(Fe^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow Fe\), \(\Delta G_{2} = -2Fy\).

Subtracting, \(Fe^{3+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Fe^{2+}\) has \(\Delta G_{3} = \Delta G_{1} - \Delta G_{2} = -3Fz + 2Fy = -1 \times F \times E^{\circ}\), so
\[E^{\circ}(Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}) = 3z - 2y\]

In the cell, \(Ag^{+}\) is reduced (cathode, \(E^{\circ} = x\)) and \(Fe^{2+}\) is oxidised (anode). Hence
\[E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = x - (3z - 2y) = x + 2y - 3z\]

Addition of aqueous \(HBr\) to an alkene begins with protonation of the double bond, so the fastest reaction belongs to the alkene that gives the most stabilised cation.

R (1-methylcyclohexene) and S (1,2-dimethylcyclohexene) are ordinary alkyl-substituted alkenes; protonation gives a simple tertiary carbocation stabilised only by hyperconjugation and induction.

P and Q are the two isomeric dihydropyrans. In Q the ring oxygen is attached directly to the double bond (an enol ether, \(O-C=C\)). Protonation at the terminal alkene carbon puts the positive charge on the carbon bearing oxygen, and the oxygen lone pair delocalises onto it to give an oxocarbenium ion:
\[O-C=C \;\xrightarrow{H^{+}}\; \overset{+}{O}=C-CH\]
This resonance stabilisation by a directly bonded oxygen is far stronger than the hyperconjugative stabilisation available to R and S.

In P the double bond is insulated from oxygen by an \(sp^{3}\) carbon, so no such resonance is possible; the electron-withdrawing inductive effect of oxygen actually makes P the least reactive.

Hence Q reacts fastest.

Two pieces of evidence fix the formula.

(i) One mole gives 3 moles of ions in water, so the complex must dissociate into one complex ion and two counter ions (a 1:2 electrolyte).

(ii) One mole gives 2 moles of \(AgCl\) with excess \(AgNO_{3}\), so exactly two chlorides are ionisable (outside the coordination sphere) and the third chloride must be coordinated.

With five ammonia ligands plus one coordinated chloride the coordination number is six, consistent with the stated octahedral geometry:
\[\left[Co(NH_{3})_{5}Cl\right]Cl_{2} \rightarrow \left[Co(NH_{3})_{5}Cl\right]^{2+} + 2Cl^{-}\]
This gives 3 ions and 2 moles of \(AgCl\), matching both observations.

Option D is a non-electrolyte, and options B and C have coordination numbers of 5 and 6 but predict the wrong ion and \(AgCl\) counts.

All four species are allylic cations, \(\overset{+}{C}H_{2}-CH=CH-X\), so they differ only in the group X at the far end of the allyl system. Because the allylic resonance places positive charge on the carbon bearing X, a group that donates a lone pair by resonance into that carbon gives the greatest extra stabilisation.

With \(X = OCH_{3}\): the alkoxy oxygen donates strongly (it has two lone pairs and nothing competing for them), producing an oxocarbenium resonance form in which every atom has a complete octet. This is the strongest stabilisation available.

With \(X = OCOCH_{3}\): the oxygen lone pair is already delocalised into the ester carbonyl, so it is much less available to the cation; the \(-I\) effect also dominates.

With \(X = F\): fluorine is a weak \(\pi\) donor (poor \(2p-2p\) size match is not the issue here, but its very strong \(-I\) effect is) and destabilises overall.

With \(X = CH_{3}\): only hyperconjugation, the weakest of the four.

The methoxy-substituted allyl cation is therefore the most stable.

Two atomic orbitals combine into molecular orbitals only if they have the same symmetry about the internuclear axis (here z), i.e. the same \(|m|\) value, otherwise the net overlap integral is exactly zero.

Classifying about z: \(s\) and \(p_{z}\) are \(\sigma\) type (\(m = 0\)); \(p_{x}, p_{y}, d_{xz}, d_{yz}\) are \(\pi\) type (\(|m| = 1\)); \(d_{xy}\) and \(d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\) are \(\delta\) type (\(|m| = 2\)).

(A) \(2p_{z}\) (\(\sigma\)) with \(2p_{x}\) (\(\pi\)): different symmetry, zero overlap.
(B) \(2s\) (\(\sigma\)) with \(2p_{x}\) (\(\pi\)): zero overlap.
(C) \(3d_{xy}\) with \(3d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\): both are \(\delta\), but they are the two mutually orthogonal components of that degenerate pair (rotated \(45^{\circ}\) from one another about z), so their overlap is also zero, exactly as for \(p_{x}\) with \(p_{y}\).
(D) \(2s\) with \(2p_{z}\): both \(\sigma\), non-zero overlap. This is the well-known s-p mixing that raises \(\sigma 2p_{z}\) above \(\pi 2p\) in \(B_{2}, C_{2}, N_{2}\).
(E) \(2p_{z}\) (\(\sigma\)) with \(3d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\) (\(\delta\)): zero overlap.

Only D leads to molecular orbital formation.

A strong oxidising agent is a species that is itself very easily reduced, i.e. one whose oxidation state is unusually high and unstable for that lanthanoid.

\(Tb^{4+}\) is \(4f^{8}\); on gaining one electron it becomes \(Tb^{3+}\), \(4f^{7}\), the specially stable half-filled configuration. This strong driving force makes \(Tb^{4+}\) a powerful oxidising agent.

\(Eu^{2+}\) is \(4f^{7}\) and tends to lose an electron to reach \(Eu^{3+}\); it is a well-known reducing agent, not an oxidant.

\(Ce^{3+}\) and \(Lu^{3+}\) are both in the normal, stable +3 state (\(Lu^{3+}\) is \(4f^{14}\), completely filled), so neither has any tendency to be reduced.

Hence \(Tb^{4+}\) is the strongest oxidising agent.

Spontaneity is governed by \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), with the process spontaneous when \(\Delta G < 0\).

The reaction is stated to be endothermic, so \(\Delta H > 0\).

It is non-spontaneous at 273 K but spontaneous at 373 K, i.e. raising the temperature turns \(\Delta G\) negative. Since the temperature enters only through the \(-T\Delta S\) term, that term must become more negative as T rises, which requires \(\Delta S > 0\).

So both \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) are positive; the reaction is entropy driven and becomes spontaneous above \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S\).

Statement I is correct: Dumas' method is indeed an estimation method for nitrogen. The organic compound is heated with copper(II) oxide in an atmosphere of \(CO_{2}\); the nitrogen is liberated as \(N_{2}\) gas, whose volume is measured over potassium hydroxide.

Statement II is incorrect: the formation of ammonium sulphate by heating the compound with concentrated \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) (in the presence of \(K_{2}SO_{4}\) and \(CuSO_{4}\)) is Kjeldahl's method, not Dumas' method. In Kjeldahl's method the \((NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}\) formed is then treated with \(NaOH\) and the ammonia distilled into a known volume of standard acid.

Hence Statement I is true and Statement II is false.

The question asks which statements are NOT true.

(A) NOT true. This is Mendeleev's old periodic law. The modern periodic law states that properties are a periodic function of atomic number, not atomic weight (Moseley).

(B) True. This is exactly the modern periodic law.

(C) NOT true. Elements with similar outer electronic configurations fall in the same GROUP (vertical column), not the same period. A period corresponds to a common value of the principal quantum number n.

(D) True. The position of an element does reflect the quantum numbers of the orbital being filled: n fixes the period, and the value of l fixes the block (s, p, d, f).

(E) NOT true. The number of elements in a period is TWICE the number of atomic orbitals being filled, because each orbital holds two electrons. For period 1 there is one orbital (1s) but two elements; for period 2 there are four orbitals (2s, three 2p) and eight elements.

The untrue statements are A, C and E.

The sugar of a nucleic acid (2-deoxy-D-ribose in DNA, D-ribose in RNA) is assessed statement by statement.

(A) True. Ribose and deoxyribose are five-carbon sugars, i.e. pentoses.

(B) False. In nucleic acids the sugar is locked in the five-membered FURANOSE ring, not the six-membered pyranose ring.

(C) True. The naturally occurring sugar is the D isomer, \(\beta\)-D-(2-deoxy)ribose.

(D) True. When free (not bonded to a base through the anomeric carbon), the sugar can open to the free aldehyde form and therefore reduces Tollens' and Fehling's reagents. It is a reducing sugar.

(E) False. The glycosidic linkage in nucleosides and nucleotides has the \(\beta\)-configuration, not \(\alpha\).

Hence A, C and D are correct.

Potassium permanganate is made from pyrolusite in two stages.

Step 1 (fusion/oxidation): \(MnO_{2}\) is fused with an alkali such as \(KOH\) in the presence of an oxidising agent, air or \(KNO_{3}\). Manganese is oxidised from +4 to +6, giving the dark green potassium manganate:
\[2MnO_{2} + 4KOH + O_{2} \rightarrow 2K_{2}MnO_{4} + 2H_{2}O\]
(with \(KNO_{3}\) supplying the oxygen).

Step 2 (disproportionation/oxidation): the manganate is then converted to permanganate, either by electrolytic oxidation or by disproportionation in acidic or neutral solution:
\[3MnO_{4}^{2-} + 4H^{+} \rightarrow 2MnO_{4}^{-} + MnO_{2} + 2H_{2}O\]

The first step therefore produces \(K_{2}MnO_{4}\).

Oxygen and sulphur belong to the same group but exist in the elemental state as very different molecular units, and it is this difference in atomicity that dominates their melting and boiling points.

Oxygen is diatomic, \(O_{2}\), a small non-polar molecule with very weak dispersion forces, so it melts at about \(-218\ ^{\circ}C\) and boils at about \(-183\ ^{\circ}C\).

Sulphur does not form stable \(p\pi-p\pi\) double bonds and instead catenates into puckered eight-membered rings, \(S_{8}\). This much larger and more polarisable unit has far stronger dispersion forces, so sulphur melts near \(119\ ^{\circ}C\) and boils near \(445\ ^{\circ}C\).

Atomic size, electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy differ between the two, but none of them accounts for a gap of several hundred degrees; the change from \(O_{2}\) to \(S_{8}\), i.e. atomicity, does.

At constant volume and temperature, partial pressure is proportional to moles, so the stoichiometry can be applied directly in pressure units.

Let the initial pressure of \(N_{2}O_{5}\) be \(P_{0}\), with no products present.
\[N_{2}O_{5} \rightarrow 2NO_{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}O_{2}\]
When 50 percent has reacted, \(0.5P_{0}\) of \(N_{2}O_{5}\) has been consumed:

remaining \(N_{2}O_{5} = 0.5P_{0}\)
formed \(NO_{2} = 2 \times 0.5P_{0} = P_{0}\)
formed \(O_{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5P_{0} = 0.25P_{0}\)

Total pressure \(= 0.5P_{0} + P_{0} + 0.25P_{0} = 1.75P_{0} = \dfrac{7}{4}P_{0}\)

So the final pressure is 7/4 times the initial pressure.

Nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl is faster when the carbonyl carbon is more electrophilic (more positive) and less hindered.

Ketone versus aldehyde: acetophenone carries an extra electron-releasing methyl group and one more bulky substituent than the aldehydes, so it is both electronically deactivated and sterically hindered. It is the least reactive of the four.

Among the three benzaldehydes, the ring substituent decides the order:
- p-nitrobenzaldehyde has a strongly electron-withdrawing \(-NO_{2}\) group (\(-I\) and \(-R\)), which increases the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon. Most reactive.
- benzaldehyde is the unsubstituted reference.
- p-tolualdehyde has an electron-releasing \(-CH_{3}\) group (\(+I\), hyperconjugation), which decreases the carbonyl's electrophilicity. Least reactive of the three aldehydes.

The increasing order is therefore
acetophenone < p-tolualdehyde < benzaldehyde < p-nitrobenzaldehyde.

Work backwards from the target x, which is 1-acetylcyclopent-1-ene: a cyclopentene ring carrying an acetyl group on one of the doubly bonded carbons (seven carbons in all).

An intramolecular aldol condensation forms the \(C=C\) of x and eliminates water, so the aldol precursor must be an open-chain dicarbonyl compound with seven carbons. Disconnecting the new \(C=C\) gives
\[CH_{3}-CO-CH_{2}-CH_{2}-CH_{2}-CH_{2}-CHO\]
(6-oxoheptanal): the carbanion alpha to the methyl ketone attacks the aldehyde carbon, closing a five-membered ring, and dehydration then places the acetyl group on the ring double bond, giving exactly x.

This dicarbonyl compound must come from ozonolysis of a cyclic alkene, which opens the ring at the \(C=C\). A ring carbon bearing a methyl group becomes a ketone and a ring \(CH\) becomes an aldehyde, so the required alkene is a \(C_{7}\) cyclohexene with the methyl group ON the double bond: 1-methylcyclohexene.
\[\text{1-methylcyclohexene} \;\xrightarrow{(i) O_{3},\ (ii) Zn/H_{2}O}\; CH_{3}-CO-CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}-CHO\]

The other options fail: 4-methylcyclohexene and 3-methylcyclohexene both give dialdehydes (no methyl ketone, so no acetyl group in the product), and methylenecyclohexane has an exocyclic double bond whose ozonolysis gives cyclohexanone plus formaldehyde, not a single dicarbonyl chain.

The freezing point of a liquid is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid equals the vapour pressure of the solid, i.e. where the two vapour-pressure curves intersect.

A correct diagram therefore needs three curves:
1. pure liquid solvent,
2. the solution, which must lie BELOW the pure solvent curve at every temperature (Raoult's law: a non-volatile solute lowers vapour pressure),
3. the frozen (solid) solvent, which intersects the other two.

The pure solvent freezes at \(T_{f}^{\circ}\), where the solid curve meets the pure liquid curve. The solution freezes at the lower temperature \(T_{f}\), where the solid curve meets the (lower) solution curve. The gap between them is \(\Delta T_{f}\), the depression in freezing point.

Only option C shows all of this correctly: the solution curve lies below the liquid solvent curve, the solid curve cuts the solution curve at \(T_{f}\) and the pure solvent curve at \(T_{f}^{\circ}\), with \(T_{f} < T_{f}^{\circ}\).

The other plots put the solution curve above the pure solvent curve, or omit the solid-solvent curve altogether, both of which contradict Raoult's law and the definition of the freezing point.

(A) True. In each of \(H_{2}O\), \(NH_{3}\) and \(CH_{4}\) the central atom has four electron domains (bond pairs plus lone pairs), so all three are \(sp^{3}\) hybridised.

(B) True. VSEPR predicts that lone pairs compress the bond angle more than bond pairs do. \(CH_{4}\) has no lone pair (\(109.5^{\circ}\)), \(NH_{3}\) has one (about \(107^{\circ}\)), \(H_{2}O\) has two (\(104.5^{\circ}\)). Listed in the stem's order the values \(104.5^{\circ}, 107.5^{\circ}, 109.5^{\circ}\) match \(H_{2}O\), \(NH_{3}\), \(CH_{4}\) respectively.

(C) True. \(CH_{4}\) is tetrahedral and its bond dipoles cancel, giving \(\mu = 0\); \(NH_{3}\) has \(\mu \approx 1.47\) D and \(H_{2}O\) has \(\mu \approx 1.85\) D. So \(CH_{4} < NH_{3} < H_{2}O\).

(D) False. \(H_{2}O\) and \(NH_{3}\) have lone pairs to donate, so they are Lewis BASES, not acids. \(CH_{4}\) has neither a lone pair nor a vacant orbital and is neither.

(E) False. The roles are reversed. In aqueous ammonia \(NH_{3} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons NH_{4}^{+} + OH^{-}\), ammonia accepts the proton (Bronsted BASE) and water donates it (Bronsted ACID). The stem states the opposite.

Hence A, B and C only.

Both conversions are \(S_{N}2\) reactions on a primary alkyl chloride; the Hughes-Ingold rules relate the solvent-polarity effect to how charge changes on going from reactants to the transition state.

Statement I: \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}Cl + HO^{-}\). The reactants are an anion plus a neutral molecule. In the transition state the negative charge is spread over the incoming \(HO\) and the departing \(Cl\), so the charge is DISPERSED. A polar solvent solvates (and thus stabilises) the concentrated charge of the free \(HO^{-}\) more than the diffuse charge of the transition state, raising the activation energy. Lowering the solvent polarity therefore speeds the reaction up. Statement I is TRUE.

Statement II: \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}Cl + R_{3}N\). Here both reactants are neutral, but the transition state and product are charged (the figure shows the quaternary ammonium salt \(R_{3}\overset{+}{N}-CH_{2}R'\;Cl^{-}\)). Charge is being CREATED, so a more polar solvent stabilises the transition state more than the reactants and accelerates the reaction. Statement II is TRUE.

Both statements are true.

Starting material: propyne, \(CH_{3}-C \equiv CH\).

Step (i) \(Hg^{2+}/H_{2}SO_{4}\): acid-catalysed hydration of the alkyne follows Markovnikov's rule, so water adds \(OH\) to the more substituted carbon. The enol tautomerises to the ketone:
\[CH_{3}-C \equiv CH \rightarrow CH_{3}-C(OH)=CH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}-CO-CH_{3}\ (\text{acetone})\]

Step (ii) \(HCN\): nucleophilic addition of cyanide to the ketone gives the cyanohydrin:
\[CH_{3}-CO-CH_{3} + HCN \rightarrow (CH_{3})_{2}C(OH)-CN\]

Step (iii) \(H_{2}/Ni\): catalytic hydrogenation reduces the nitrile all the way to a primary amine (the tertiary alcohol is untouched):
\[(CH_{3})_{2}C(OH)-CN + 2H_{2} \rightarrow (CH_{3})_{2}C(OH)-CH_{2}-NH_{2}\]

Product A is 1-amino-2-methylpropan-2-ol, i.e. \(CH_{3}-C(OH)(CH_{3})-CH_{2}-NH_{2}\), which is option B.

Option A has the \(OH\) and \(NH_{2}\) interchanged, and options C and D have an unbranched butane skeleton that cannot arise from acetone.

For
\[\tfrac{1}{2}X_{2} + \tfrac{5}{2}Y_{2} \rightarrow XY_{5}\]
the standard entropy change is
\[\Delta S^{\circ} = S^{\circ}(XY_{5}) - \left[\tfrac{1}{2}S^{\circ}(X_{2}) + \tfrac{5}{2}S^{\circ}(Y_{2})\right]\]
\[\Delta S^{\circ} = 110 - \left[\tfrac{1}{2}(70) + \tfrac{5}{2}(50)\right] = 110 - (35 + 125) = -50\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}\]

At equilibrium \(\Delta G^{\circ} = 0\), so \(\Delta H^{\circ} = T\Delta S^{\circ}\):
\[T = \frac{\Delta H^{\circ}}{\Delta S^{\circ}} = \frac{-35000\ J\ mol^{-1}}{-50\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} = 700\ K\]

(The signs are consistent: with both \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) negative, the reaction is spontaneous below 700 K and non-spontaneous above it.)

\[C_{6}H_{5}COOH + NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow C_{6}H_{5}COONa + H_{2}O + CO_{2}\]

The reaction is 1:1 in acid and \(CO_{2}\).

So 0.5 mol of benzoic acid reacted. Its molar mass is \(7(12) + 6(1) + 2(16) = 84 + 6 + 32 = 122\ g\ mol^{-1}\).

Potassium hexacyanoferrate(II), \(K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]\), is a confirmatory reagent for several cations, each giving a characteristically coloured insoluble hexacyanoferrate:

\(Cu^{2+}\): chocolate-brown (reddish-brown) \(Cu_{2}[Fe(CN)_{6}]\). Gives a precipitate.
\(Fe^{3+}\): the intense Prussian blue \(Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}\). Gives a precipitate.
\(Zn^{2+}\): white to bluish-white \(K_{2}Zn_{3}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{2}\). Gives a precipitate.
\(Ba^{2+}\): white, sparingly soluble \(Ba_{2}[Fe(CN)_{6}]\). Gives a precipitate.

The remaining three do not:
\(NH_{4}^{+}\) forms only the freely soluble ammonium salt (it is identified by Nessler's reagent instead).
\(Mg^{2+}\) and \(Ca^{2+}\) form hexacyanoferrates that are essentially soluble under these conditions, so no characteristic precipitate is obtained; they are identified by ammonium phosphate and ammonium oxalate respectively.

Hence 4 cations give a characteristic precipitate.

This is a limiting-reagent calculation on
\[Fe_{3}O_{4(s)} + 4CO_{(g)} \rightarrow 3Fe_{(l)} + 4CO_{2(g)}\]

Moles supplied (working in grams):
\[n(Fe_{3}O_{4}) = \frac{2.32 \times 10^{6}}{232} = 1.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{mol}\]
\[n(CO) = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{5}}{28} = 1.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{mol}\]

The equation needs 4 mol of \(CO\) per mol of \(Fe_{3}O_{4}\), i.e. \(4 \times 10^{4}\) mol of \(CO\), but only \(1 \times 10^{4}\) mol is available. Carbon monoxide is therefore the limiting reagent (only one quarter of the oxide can be reduced).

From the stoichiometry, 4 mol \(CO\) give 3 mol \(Fe\):
\[n(Fe) = \frac{3}{4} \times 1.0 \times 10^{4} = 7.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{mol}\]
\[m(Fe) = 7.5 \times 10^{3} \times 56 = 4.2 \times 10^{5}\ g = 420\ kg\]

So \(x = 420\).

A reducing agent is itself oxidised, so the strongest reducing agent is the REDUCED member of the couple with the most negative standard reduction potential (its reverse, oxidation, potential is then the most positive).

Ranking the given reduction potentials:
\(E^{\circ}(MnO_{4}^{-}/Mn^{2+}) = +1.51\ V\)
\(E^{\circ}(Cl_{2}/Cl^{-}) = +1.36\ V\)
\(E^{\circ}(Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}/Cr^{3+}) = +1.33\ V\)
\(E^{\circ}(Cr^{3+}/Cr) = -0.74\ V\)

The only negative value belongs to the \(Cr^{3+}/Cr\) couple, so metallic \(Cr\) is the species most readily oxidised:
\[Cr \rightarrow Cr^{3+} + 3e^{-},\qquad E^{\circ}_{ox} = +0.74\ V\]

The other candidates are all at or near their highest accessible oxidation states in a strongly oxidising couple: \(MnO_{4}^{-}\) and \(Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}\) are oxidising agents, and \(Cl^{-}\) and \(Mn^{2+}\) are much harder to oxidise than \(Cr\) (their couples sit at +1.36 V and +1.51 V).

Hence \(Cr\) is the strongest reducing agent.

Statement I (figure: \(t_{1/2}\) plotted against \([R]_{0}\) as a horizontal line). For a first order reaction \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\), which contains no concentration term, so the half-life is independent of the initial concentration and the plot is indeed a horizontal straight line. The hydrogen atom is a one-electron system, so there is no inter-electronic repulsion and no screening. Its orbital energies depend ONLY on the principal quantum number:
\[E_{n} = -\frac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ eV\]
All orbitals with the same n are exactly degenerate: \(2s = 2p\), \(3s = 3p = 3d\), and so on. (The \((n+l)\) rule applies to multi-electron atoms, not to hydrogen.)

Classifying the listed orbitals:
(A) 4s, \(n = 4\)
(B) \(3p_{x}\), \(n = 3\)
(C) \(3d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\), \(n = 3\)
(D) \(3d_{z^{2}}\), \(n = 3\)
(E) \(4p_{z}\), \(n = 4\)

The lowest energy corresponds to the smallest n, which is \(n = 3\). So B, C and D are all degenerate and all lie lowest; A and E are higher.

Hence the answer is (B), (C) and (D) only.

The temperature rise is \(\Delta T = q/(m \times c)\), so it depends both on the heat released (which depends on the moles actually neutralised and on the enthalpy of neutralisation) and inversely on the total mass of solution.

For a weak acid such as \(CH_{3}COOH\) part of that energy is consumed in ionising the acid, so the value is smaller in magnitude (about \(-55.9\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)).

Taking all solutions as 1 M and comparing (heat released) divided by (total volume):

(A) 30 mL \(HCl\) + 30 mL \(NaOH\): 0.030 mol neutralised, total 60 mL. \(q/V \propto (0.030 \times 57.1)/60 = 0.0286\)
(B) 30 mL \(CH_{3}COOH\) + 30 mL \(NaOH\): 0.030 mol, total 60 mL, but weaker heat release. \(\propto (0.030 \times 55.9)/60 = 0.0280\)
(C) 50 mL \(HCl\) + 20 mL \(NaOH\): \(NaOH\) limits to 0.020 mol, total 70 mL. \(\propto (0.020 \times 57.1)/70 = 0.0163\)
(D) 45 mL \(CH_{3}COOH\) + 25 mL \(NaOH\): \(NaOH\) limits to 0.025 mol, total 70 mL. \(\propto (0.025 \times 55.9)/70 = 0.0200\)

Option A gives the largest value: it combines the maximum number of moles neutralised with the smallest total volume and the full strong-acid/strong-base enthalpy. Hence A shows the largest increase in temperature.

The configuration \(t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{1}\) accounts for four \(d\) electrons, i.e. a \(d^{4}\) octahedral metal ion.

For a \(d^{4}\) ion the fourth electron has a choice: pair up in a \(t_{2g}\) orbital (cost = pairing energy P) or occupy a higher \(e_{g}\) orbital (cost = \(\Delta_{o}\)). It goes into \(e_{g}\) only when
\[\Delta_{o} < P\]
which is the condition for a WEAK field ligand.

The result, \(t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{1}\), has four unpaired electrons, the maximum possible for \(d^{4}\), so it is a HIGH SPIN complex.

(By contrast a strong field ligand, \(\Delta_{o} > P\), would force the low-spin configuration \(t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{0}\) with only two unpaired electrons.)

Hence: weak field ligand, high spin complex.

All four entries are classical named methods for making an aldehyde, distinguished by their starting material and reagent.

(B) Benzoyl chloride with \(H_{2}\) over palladium poisoned with barium sulphate gives benzaldehyde. The poisoned catalyst stops the reduction at the aldehyde stage instead of going on to the alcohol. This is ROSENMUND reduction -> (III).
